script.opening: (Mother speaks; Rory sits next to her, head down, fiddling with his sleeve.) "Rory's 7 and still wetting the bed most nights. His dad's getting frustrated — says he's far too old for this and should know better. We've tried lifting him, telling him off, taking away drinks … nothing works. Is there something wrong with him? It's causing rows at home."

facts.text: Five or six nights a week, large wet patches, doesn't wake. "He's never really been dry at night" — never dry for more than a few nights in a row.
(Rory, if asked directly) "No" — no wetting or rushing in the day. No pain passing urine. Not thirsty all the time; no weight loss.
(Rory shrugs.) Mum: "I don't really know — he goes on his own now." If asked further: Rory says it "sometimes hurts" and he goes every few days.
"No, nothing like that" — no snoring or stopping breathing, no back problems, walks and runs normally, no fevers or infections.
"We cut his drinks after tea." Drinks very little at school (doesn't like the toilets), two cans of cola a week. "Nothing's changed — apart from the arguing about this."
Dad wet the bed until he was 9 (Mum knows; Dad doesn't talk about it). Lives with Mum, Dad and sister (4). No recent upsets, no bullying, no social worker. Rory has stopped going to sleepovers.
(Rory, quietly, if asked kindly) "Embarrassed. I don't want anyone to know." Wants to go on a Cubs camp in 3 months.
No medicines, no allergies, healthy, growing well.

Mum is worried and tired; Rory is shy and only answers if the doctor talks to him directly and kindly. If the doctor talks only to Mum, Rory stays silent. If asked what she fears: "That something's wrong with him. And the rows — his dad gets so cross. I just want it to stop." Relieved: "So it really isn't him being lazy?" Rory chooses: "The alarm. But not if it wakes everyone up." Mum asks for a leaflet for Dad: "He might listen to a doctor."

ice.ideas: (Mother) "Maybe something's wrong with him — or he's too old and should know better." (Rory) "It's my fault."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — rows at home and Dad's anger; Rory's shame and missing sleepovers; Mum wants to hear he is normal.
ice.expectations: "Something to make it stop." (Rory) To go on the Cubs camp.

cues: "His dad's getting frustrated." — family conflict to defuse.
(Rory) "Embarrassed." — needs reassurance it isn't his fault.
"We cut his drinks after tea." — invites advice on fluids.

checkpoints.text: DE-SHAMES first — states clearly to parent AND child that bedwetting at 7 is common, NOT the child’s fault and treatable — and stops punitive measures (telling off, restricting drinks, lifting), protecting the child from blame
Takes a focused history distinguishing PRIMARY vs SECONDARY enuresis, and covering daytime symptoms, fluids/caffeine, constipation, sleep, family history and psychosocial stressors

Excludes/treats contributors and red flags: CONSTIPATION (reversible, treat it), UTI (urinalysis only when indicated, not routinely — CG111), DIABETES (polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss — same-day glucose if suggestive), daytime bladder dysfunction, neurological/spinal signs, safeguarding/emotional triggers

Manages per NICE CG111: demystify, address the BASICS (adequate drinks spread through the day, avoid caffeine, toileting, constipation, stop punishment/lifting), then ENURESIS ALARM as first-line for motivated families, with DESMOPRESSIN as an option (short-term/sleepovers/alarm unsuitable) and its safety rule explained (no fluids from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the dose — hyponatraemia; omit if vomiting or diarrhoea)
Uses positive REWARD systems for agreed behaviours (good drinking/toileting/helping) NOT for dry nights, and sets realistic expectations (alarms take weeks, gradual success)

Engages RORY directly and kindly, lifts the blame, and helps the mother defuse the absent father’s frustration and the family conflict (an explanation or note she can share, without criticising him in front of Rory) — protecting the child’s self-esteem
Reassures the mother he is normal, educates the family compassionately, and watches for emotional impact/secondary causes

Safety-nets and follows up: treat constipation/exclude diabetes, alarm/desmopressin plan with review, realistic timescales, and support — effective, de-shaming care that protects the child (exclude diabetes)

worked.txt: "Rory, this is really common — lots of children your age still wet the bed, and it is absolutely not your fault. You’re not lazy and you’re not naughty. And the good news is we can usually fix it together. (To mum) Telling off and taking away drinks actually make it harder, so let’s stop those."

"Has he ever been dry at night, or did it come back after being dry? Any wetting or rushing in the daytime? How are his poos — is he constipated? Any extra thirst or weeing a lot in the day? … That helps me find what’s driving it."

"Constipation is a really common, fixable cause — so we’ll sort that. As there are no daytime problems, no signs of infection and no extra thirst, he doesn’t need a urine test today — we’d test if any of those appear. A two-week bladder and bowel diary will help us see the pattern."

"First, the basics: good drinks spread through the day rather than cutting them, avoid fizzy or caffeine drinks, a wee before bed, and no lifting him at night. Then the best long-term fix is a bedwetting alarm — it teaches his body to wake. It takes a few weeks of teamwork, but it works well."

"There’s also a medicine that can keep him dry quickly — handy for sleepovers — which we can use too; with it, he mustn’t drink from an hour before the tablet until the morning, because too much fluid with it can be dangerous, and he skips it if he’s being sick or has diarrhoea. And a reward chart — but for doing his part, like drinking well and helping change the sheets, not for dry nights, because he can’t control those yet."

"Rory, you’re going to be the captain of this plan. (To mum) Would a short note for his dad help, explaining it isn’t Rory’s fault? No blame, lots of encouragement; that matters as much as the alarm. Come back if it’s not improving, or if you notice lots of thirst or weight loss, and let’s review in a few weeks."

f.learning: Nocturnal enuresis at 7 must be managed without shame: it is common (affecting a significant minority of children), not the child’s fault, not laziness or naughtiness, and very treatable — so the first and central task is to say so clearly to both parent and child, stop the counterproductive and harmful responses (telling off, restricting drinks, lifting), protect the child from blame, and engage the embarrassed child kindly and directly. Take a focused history distinguishing primary (never dry) from secondary (dry then wetting again, more likely to have an emotional or medical trigger), and covering daytime symptoms (urgency/frequency/daytime wetting suggesting bladder dysfunction), fluid and caffeine intake/timing, constipation, sleep/snoring, family history (often positive) and psychosocial stressors. Exclude and treat contributors and red flags — constipation (a very common, reversible cause that often resolves the enuresis when treated), UTI (urinalysis only when indicated, not routinely — NICE CG111), diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss — same-day glucose if suggestive, never miss new-onset type 1, NICE NG18), daytime bladder dysfunction, neurological/spinal signs, and safeguarding/emotional triggers for secondary enuresis. Manage per NICE CG111: demystify and reassure, address the basics first (adequate drinks spread through the day rather than restricted, avoid caffeine, regular toileting, treat constipation, stop punishment and lifting), then offer an enuresis alarm as first-line for a motivated child/family (best long-term cure rates, needs weeks of commitment), with desmopressin as an option for rapid/short-term results, sleepovers, or where an alarm is unsuitable or has failed (dose per BNFC, with fluid restricted from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the dose because of hyponatraemia risk, and omitted during vomiting or diarrhoea); use reward systems for agreed behaviours (good drinking, toileting, helping with sheets) not for dry nights, which the child cannot control. Engage the child as owner of the plan, set realistic expectations, and — given the loaded dynamic of the father’s frustration, family rows and the child’s shame — lift the blame, educate the family (offering the mother an explanation she can share with the absent father), and protect the child’s wellbeing as much as treating the symptom, watching for emotional impact or secondary causes. Exclude diabetes.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG111 (2010) — Bedwetting in under 19s · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect · NICE NG18 — Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people · BNFC
knowledge.summary: Bedwetting at 7 is common, involuntary and treatable. Remove the blame, look for contributors (constipation, daytime symptoms, UTI, diabetes, stressors), then choose an alarm for lasting cure or desmopressin for rapid, short-term control.

points.t: NICE CG111: reassure that bedwetting is not the child’s fault and punitive measures should not be used. Do not exclude younger children from management on the basis of age alone.

NICE CG111: primary (never dry) or secondary (wetting after a period of being dry), frequency, daytime symptoms, fluid intake, constipation and soiling, developmental or emotional problems, family pressures, and the impact on the child.

NICE CG111: urinalysis is not routine. Test the urine if the wetting started in the last few days or weeks, there are daytime symptoms, signs of ill health, or symptoms of UTI or diabetes. New thirst, polyuria or weight loss needs a same-day glucose check (NICE NG18).

NICE CG111: adequate drinks spread through the day, avoid caffeine, regular toileting including before bed, treat constipation. Lifting or waking may help in the short term but does not promote long-term dryness.

NICE CG111: an alarm is first-line for a motivated family when advice has not worked; review at 4 weeks and continue until at least 2 weeks of uninterrupted dry nights. Desmopressin when rapid or short-term control is the priority, or an alarm is unsuitable (dose per BNFC).

BNFC: restrict fluid from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the dose because of the risk of hyponatraemia; omit the dose if the child is vomiting or has diarrhoea. Rewards for agreed behaviours, not for dry nights (NICE CG111).

Primary monosymptomatic enuresis versus daytime bladder dysfunction, constipation, UTI, diabetes and emotional triggers.

Primary nocturnal enuresis without daytime symptoms, explained without blame.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Idea (too old, should know better); concern (something wrong, family rows); expectation (make it stop).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Vaughan, and hello Rory. Thanks for coming on together. What would you like to talk about today?
model.why: Greets and includes the child from the start

model.text: Rory’s 7 and still wetting the bed most nights. His dad says he’s far too old and should know better. We’ve tried lifting him, telling him off, taking away drinks — nothing works. Is there something wrong with him? It’s causing rows.

Thank you. Before anything else, Rory — lots of children your age wet the bed. It is not your fault, and it isn’t something you’re doing on purpose. Is it okay if I ask some questions, and some of them to you?
model.why: De-shames the child directly before gathering data

model.text: (Rory nods.)
Then I’ll explain what I think is going on, and we’ll make a plan that works for your family.
Has Rory ever been dry at night for a good stretch, say six months, or has it always been like this?
He’s never really been dry at night.
Rory, in the daytime, do you ever have to rush to the toilet, or have little accidents?
model.why: Daytime symptoms asked of the child

model.text: (Rory) No.
And your poos — are they ever hard, or do they hurt?
model.why: Constipation screen, a common reversible contributor

model.text: (Rory shrugs.) Mum: I don’t really know — he goes on his own now.
That’s fine — we can keep a note for a week or two. Has he been extra thirsty lately, weeing a lot in the day, losing weight, or seeming tired and unwell?
No, nothing like that.
What does he usually drink in the day, and when? And has anything changed or been difficult for him recently — at school or at home?
We cut his drinks after tea. Nothing’s changed — apart from the arguing about this.
Rory, how does it make you feel?
model.why: Explores the impact on the child directly

model.text: (Rory, quietly) Embarrassed. I don’t want anyone to know.
That makes sense, and thank you for telling me. It stays between us and your family. Mrs Vaughan, what’s been worrying you most?
model.why: Validates the child and moves to the parent’s concern

model.text: That something’s wrong with him. And the rows — his dad gets so cross. I just want it to stop.

Nothing you’ve told me suggests anything serious. Bedwetting at 7 is common. Usually the body makes a lot of wee at night and the bladder signal isn’t yet strong enough to wake him. He’s asleep — he can’t choose to be dry, so telling off doesn’t help and can make it harder.
model.why: Explains the mechanism and stops punitive measures

model.text: So it really isn’t him being lazy?

It really isn’t. There’s no need for a urine test today, because there are no daytime problems or signs of infection or diabetes. What I would like is a two-week diary — drinks, wees, poos and wet or dry nights. If the diary shows constipation, treating that sometimes fixes the wetting on its own.
model.why: CG111-consistent testing and a diary to look for contributors

model.text: We can do that.

The basics: plenty of drinks spread through the day rather than cutting them, avoid fizzy or caffeine drinks, a wee before bed, and stop lifting him. Lifting can give a dry sheet but doesn’t teach his body to wake.
model.why: CG111 basic advice, replacing counterproductive measures

model.text: Okay. And if that doesn’t work?

Then there are two good options. A bedwetting alarm that goes off at the first drop and gradually teaches his brain to wake — it has the best long-term success but takes several weeks of teamwork. Or a tablet at bedtime called desmopressin that reduces the wee made overnight — quick, and useful for sleepovers, but it often comes back when stopped. With the tablet, he mustn’t drink from an hour before until the morning, because too much fluid with it can be dangerous.
model.why: Alarm versus desmopressin by goal, with the key fluid safety rule

model.text: Rory, what do you think?
(Rory) The alarm. But not if it wakes everyone up.

Good thinking — we’ll talk about that at review. And a reward chart, Rory, but for the things you can do: drinking well in the day, a wee before bed, helping change the sheets. Not for dry nights, because they’ll come later. You’re the captain of this plan.
model.why: Rewards behaviours not outcomes; makes the child the owner

model.text: (Rory smiles.)
Mrs Vaughan, would it help if I wrote a short note for Rory’s dad explaining that this isn’t Rory’s fault and that telling off makes it harder? Encouragement at home matters as much as the alarm.
model.why: Addresses the family conflict without blaming the absent parent

model.text: Yes, please. He might listen to a doctor.

Let’s review with the diary in two to three weeks. Contact us sooner if he becomes very thirsty, is weeing much more in the day, loses weight or seems unwell — that needs a same-day check. Also if he starts wetting in the day, or it hurts to wee.
model.why: Specific safety-net for diabetes and UTI with a defined review

model.text: Thirsty, weight loss, daytime wetting. Got it.
Rory, what are you going to tell your dad about why this happens?
(Rory) That my body is still learning to wake up. And it’s not my fault.
Perfect. That’s exactly it.
model.why: Reinforces the key message and closes

social.t: Frustration and blame at home increase shame and can worsen wetting. Offering the family a clear explanation to share helps bring all carers on side.
Fear of discovery limits friendships. Desmopressin is useful for short-term control around these events.

legal.t: NICE CG89: consider child maltreatment if a child is punished for wetting despite professional advice that it is involuntary. Advise clearly that it is involuntary and record that advice.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance: involve children in decisions about their care at a level they understand. Let Rory help choose between options.
Address the father’s view respectfully without criticising him in front of the child; offer written information for the family.

community.t: School nurse and local children’s continence services provide alarms and support. ERIC, The Children’s Bowel and Bladder Charity, has family and child resources.

redFlags: Thirst, polyuria, weight loss or tiredness — same-day glucose for new type 1 diabetes
Secondary onset, daytime wetting, dysuria — UTI, bladder dysfunction or emotional trigger
Punitive responses or other concerns about the child’s welfare (NICE CG89)
psychosocial: Father’s frustration and rows at home
Rory’s embarrassment and fear of others knowing
What has already been tried, and how motivated the family is for an alarm
ice: Idea: “He’s too old for this and should know better”
Concern: “Is there something wrong with him?”; the family rows
Expectation: a way to make it stop

playbook.diagnosis: Primary nocturnal enuresis without daytime symptoms. No features of UTI or diabetes, so no tests today; a bladder and bowel diary looks for constipation and fluid patterns.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “At night his body makes quite a lot of wee, and the signal from his bladder isn’t yet strong enough to wake him. He’s fast asleep — he can’t choose to be dry.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked whether something’s wrong with him — nothing you’ve told me suggests that. And Rory, being embarrassed makes total sense, but lots of children in your class will be dealing with the same thing.”
management.psychosocial: Stop punishment and lifting; give the family an explanation to share with Rory’s father; make Rory the owner of the plan and reward behaviours he controls.
sharedPlan: Two-week diary; drinks spread through the day; avoid caffeine; wee before bed
Treat constipation if the diary or examination suggests it
Alarm first-line if the basics fail; desmopressin for rapid or short-term control, with the fluid restriction
safetyNet: Same-day review for thirst, polyuria, weight loss or feeling unwell
Review with the diary in two to three weeks; alarm review at 4 weeks if started

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards a consultation that removes shame from a child. Candidates know about alarms; they fail by talking over the child, missing diabetes, or giving desmopressin without its safety rule.

items.fail: Talking only to the mother while Rory sits silently.
items.why: “Did not involve the child” is a recurring failing statement; the child’s shame is the centre of the case.
items.fix: Tell Rory it isn’t his fault in the first minute, ask him some questions directly, and let him help choose the plan.

items.fail: Not asking about thirst, polyuria or weight loss.
items.why: New-onset type 1 diabetes can present with wetting; missing it is a serious-disease fail.
items.fix: One question covers it — and a same-day glucose if any are present.

items.fail: Endorsing evening fluid restriction and lifting.
items.why: NICE CG111 advises adequate drinks through the day and notes that lifting does not promote long-term dryness.
items.fix: “Drinks spread through the day, avoid caffeine, a wee before bed, and stop lifting.”

items.fail: Offering desmopressin without the fluid restriction.
items.why: Hyponatraemia is the key safety issue with desmopressin; examiners expect it named in plain words.
items.fix: “No drinks from an hour before the tablet until the morning, and skip it if he’s being sick or has diarrhoea.”

items.fail: Criticising the father, or ignoring him entirely.
items.why: Blaming an absent parent in front of the child adds conflict; ignoring him leaves the punitive dynamic untouched.
items.fix: Offer an explanation the family can share: “It isn’t Rory’s fault, and encouragement works better than telling off.”

items.fail: Ending with “come back if it doesn’t get better”.
items.why: Vague follow-up and safety-netting fail Global Skills.
items.fix: Diary review in two to three weeks, alarm review at 4 weeks, and named same-day symptoms.

Primary or secondary; daytime symptoms; poos; thirst, weight loss, polyuria; drinks; stressors. Ask Rory some questions directly.
How Rory feels; what worries mum; the father’s frustration and the rows.
Why it happens; no test unless indicated; diary. Basics, stop lifting and punishment. Alarm versus desmopressin by goal. Rewards for behaviours.
Thirst, weight loss, daytime wetting. Review with diary. Rory explains it back.

wordPics.fail: Talks only to the mother; accepts the “too old” framing or offers no reassurance; misses the diabetes screen; prescribes desmopressin without the fluid rule; rewards dry nights; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: De-shames, takes a focused history including constipation and diabetes, gives CG111 basic advice, offers alarm or desmopressin appropriately and arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: speaks to Rory directly and early; lets him choose; rewards behaviours; explains desmopressin safety in plain words; tests only when indicated; gives the family a way to bring dad on side; Rory leaves less ashamed.

SCA_MODELS.why: Alarm versus desmopressin by goal, with the key fluid safety rule

SCA_MODELS.text: Rory, what do you think?
(Rory) The alarm. But not if it wakes everyone up.

Good thinking — we’ll talk about that at review. And a reward chart, Rory, but for the things you can do: drinking well in the day, a wee before bed, helping change the sheets. Not for dry nights, because they’ll come later. You’re the captain of this plan.
SCA_MODELS.why: Rewards behaviours not outcomes; makes the child the owner

SCA_MODELS.text: (Rory smiles.)
Mrs Vaughan, would it help if I wrote a short note for Rory’s dad explaining that this isn’t Rory’s fault and that telling off makes it harder? Encouragement at home matters as much as the alarm.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the family conflict without blaming the absent parent

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, please. He might listen to a doctor.

Let’s review with the diary in two to three weeks. Contact us sooner if he becomes very thirsty, is weeing much more in the day, loses weight or seems unwell — that needs a same-day check. Also if he starts wetting in the day, or it hurts to wee.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for diabetes and UTI with a defined review

SCA_MODELS.text: Thirsty, weight loss, daytime wetting. Got it.
Rory, what are you going to tell your dad about why this happens?
(Rory) That my body is still learning to wake up. And it’s not my fault.
Perfect. That’s exactly it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reinforces the key message and closes

SCA_STEM.name: Rory Vaughan
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Wets the bed most nights. Family has tried lifting him at night, telling him off and cutting down drinks, without success.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother asking whether something is wrong with him; bedwetting is causing rows at home.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG111 (2010) — Bedwetting in under 19s · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect · NICE NG18 — Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people · BNFC
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Bedwetting at 7 is common, involuntary and treatable. Remove the blame, look for contributors (constipation, daytime symptoms, UTI, diabetes, stressors), then choose an alarm for lasting cure or desmopressin for rapid, short-term control.

points.t: NICE CG111: reassure that bedwetting is not the child’s fault and punitive measures should not be used. Do not exclude younger children from management on the basis of age alone.

NICE CG111: primary (never dry) or secondary (wetting after a period of being dry), frequency, daytime symptoms, fluid intake, constipation and soiling, developmental or emotional problems, family pressures, and the impact on the child.

NICE CG111: urinalysis is not routine. Test the urine if the wetting started in the last few days or weeks, there are daytime symptoms, signs of ill health, or symptoms of UTI or diabetes. New thirst, polyuria or weight loss needs a same-day glucose check (NICE NG18).

NICE CG111: adequate drinks spread through the day, avoid caffeine, regular toileting including before bed, treat constipation. Lifting or waking may help in the short term but does not promote long-term dryness.

NICE CG111: an alarm is first-line for a motivated family when advice has not worked; review at 4 weeks and continue until at least 2 weeks of uninterrupted dry nights. Desmopressin when rapid or short-term control is the priority, or an alarm is unsuitable (dose per BNFC).

BNFC: restrict fluid from 1 hour before to 8 hours after the dose because of the risk of hyponatraemia; omit the dose if the child is vomiting or has diarrhoea. Rewards for agreed behaviours, not for dry nights (NICE CG111).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to mother and child; let the mother describe what has been tried and the rows at home.
Father’s frustration, family conflict, punitive responses, school and home stressors, impact on Rory.
Picked up the child’s embarrassment and the mother’s “is there something wrong with him?”, and responded to both.
Idea (too old, should know better); concern (something wrong, family rows); expectation (make it stop).
Two-week bladder and bowel diary; urinalysis and glucose only when CG111 or NG18 features are present; examine if constipation or neurological concern.
Primary monosymptomatic enuresis versus daytime bladder dysfunction, constipation, UTI, diabetes and emotional triggers.
Asked about thirst, polyuria, weight loss, daytime symptoms and secondary onset; safeguarding awareness given punitive responses.
Primary nocturnal enuresis without daytime symptoms, explained without blame.
CG111 basics; stop lifting and punishment; alarm first-line if basics fail; desmopressin as an option with the fluid restriction explained.
Constipation looked for and treated if found; fluids spread through the day; father’s response addressed.
Review with diary in two to three weeks; same-day review for thirst, polyuria, weight loss; alarm review at 4 weeks if started.

social.t: Frustration and blame at home increase shame and can worsen wetting. Offering the family a clear explanation to share helps bring all carers on side.
Fear of discovery limits friendships. Desmopressin is useful for short-term control around these events.

legal.t: NICE CG89: consider child maltreatment if a child is punished for wetting despite professional advice that it is involuntary. Advise clearly that it is involuntary and record that advice.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years guidance: involve children in decisions about their care at a level they understand. Let Rory help choose between options.
Address the father’s view respectfully without criticising him in front of the child; offer written information for the family.

community.t: School nurse and local children’s continence services provide alarms and support. ERIC, The Children’s Bowel and Bladder Charity, has family and child resources.

redFlags: Thirst, polyuria, weight loss or tiredness — same-day glucose for new type 1 diabetes
Secondary onset, daytime wetting, dysuria — UTI, bladder dysfunction or emotional trigger
Punitive responses or other concerns about the child’s welfare (NICE CG89)
psychosocial: Father’s frustration and rows at home
Rory’s embarrassment and fear of others knowing
What has already been tried, and how motivated the family is for an alarm
ice: Idea: “He’s too old for this and should know better”
Concern: “Is there something wrong with him?”; the family rows
Expectation: a way to make it stop

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Primary nocturnal enuresis without daytime symptoms. No features of UTI or diabetes, so no tests today; a bladder and bowel diary looks for constipation and fluid patterns.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “At night his body makes quite a lot of wee, and the signal from his bladder isn’t yet strong enough to wake him. He’s fast asleep — he can’t choose to be dry.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked whether something’s wrong with him — nothing you’ve told me suggests that. And Rory, being embarrassed makes total sense, but lots of children in your class will be dealing with the same thing.”
management.psychosocial: Stop punishment and lifting; give the family an explanation to share with Rory’s father; make Rory the owner of the plan and reward behaviours he controls.
sharedPlan: Two-week diary; drinks spread through the day; avoid caffeine; wee before bed
Treat constipation if the diary or examination suggests it
Alarm first-line if the basics fail; desmopressin for rapid or short-term control, with the fluid restriction
safetyNet: Same-day review for thirst, polyuria, weight loss or feeling unwell
Review with the diary in two to three weeks; alarm review at 4 weeks if started

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards a consultation that removes shame from a child. Candidates know about alarms; they fail by talking over the child, missing diabetes, or giving desmopressin without its safety rule.

items.fail: Talking only to the mother while Rory sits silently.
items.why: “Did not involve the child” is a recurring failing statement; the child’s shame is the centre of the case.
items.fix: Tell Rory it isn’t his fault in the first minute, ask him some questions directly, and let him help choose the plan.

items.fail: Not asking about thirst, polyuria or weight loss.
items.why: New-onset type 1 diabetes can present with wetting; missing it is a serious-disease fail.
items.fix: One question covers it — and a same-day glucose if any are present.

items.fail: Endorsing evening fluid restriction and lifting.
items.why: NICE CG111 advises adequate drinks through the day and notes that lifting does not promote long-term dryness.
items.fix: “Drinks spread through the day, avoid caffeine, a wee before bed, and stop lifting.”

items.fail: Offering desmopressin without the fluid restriction.
items.why: Hyponatraemia is the key safety issue with desmopressin; examiners expect it named in plain words.
items.fix: “No drinks from an hour before the tablet until the morning, and skip it if he’s being sick or has diarrhoea.”

items.fail: Criticising the father, or ignoring him entirely.
items.why: Blaming an absent parent in front of the child adds conflict; ignoring him leaves the punitive dynamic untouched.
items.fix: Offer an explanation the family can share: “It isn’t Rory’s fault, and encouragement works better than telling off.”

items.fail: Ending with “come back if it doesn’t get better”.
items.why: Vague follow-up and safety-netting fail Global Skills.
items.fix: Diary review in two to three weeks, alarm review at 4 weeks, and named same-day symptoms.
